meta.title: Conflict Watchlist
meta.notes: Fully automated register: a scheduled open-source review rewrites this file daily (procedure in docs/WATCHLIST-REVIEW.md) and an hourly GitHub Action refreshes the live reporting feed (watchlist-live.json) from GDELT. Every comparison the dashboard shows (state moves, changed dimensions, the attention-score bonuses) is made against the register as it stood compareDays (7) days ago, taken from each item's `snapshots` (one entry per review: date, state and the five dimensions). Each review: (1) set reviewDate/previousReviewDate, (2) for every item set the new `now` on the five dimensions and the new `state`, then append today's snapshot (keep the last 60), (3) rewrite `status` (`summary`: plain-language current status whose first sentence states the newest development; `sources`: 2–3 links to the newest reporting), `whyNow`, `topic` and `whyMatters` (stable framing, revise only on a phase change), `changes` (dated bullets covering the last 7 days: keep those still inside the window, add today's, drop older ones), `next`, `ignore` and `sources`, (4) record any state move in `history` and keep `timeline` (4–8 dated one-line events of the current phase, chronological) current. The dashboard derives attention rank, movements, changed-dimension flags, staleness, coverage surges — do not type those in. `next` holds named, checkable indicators.

phase.label: Conflict phase
phase.desc: A short label for the stage the conflict is in (for example attritional war, ceasefire without implementation, grey-zone contest). It sits under the current-status summary and shows the label from 7 days ago when it changed.

escalation.label: Escalation risk
escalation.desc: How likely a step up in intensity or a change of phase is in the coming weeks.

levels.Low: Stable; no live trigger and restraints hold.
levels.Moderate: Triggers exist (deadlines, disputes, incidents) but restraints are holding.
levels.High: Active exchanges or a named trigger that is likely to fire; a phase change is plausible within weeks.
levels.Severe: Active war or ongoing kinetic exchange with strategic stakes (major shipping lanes, energy, great-power forces).

tempo.label: Operational tempo
tempo.desc: How much military activity is actually happening in the review window.

levels.Medium: Recurring incidents or steady, limited operations (patrols, fortification, occasional strikes).
levels.High: Daily strikes or operations across fronts.

adaptation.label: Adaptation behaviour
adaptation.desc: How much new tactical or technical behaviour appeared in the window; this is where the Army learning sits.

levels.Low: Both sides are using the same methods as before.
levels.High: Novel, repeatable adaptations appeared (new weapons employment, counter-measures, doctrine shifts).

sgExposure.label: Singapore exposure
sgExposure.desc: How directly the conflict touches Singapore's interests. Not shown as a register column; it still feeds the attention score and the expanded row.

levels.Moderate: An ASEAN or diplomatic role, observer contributions, or supply-chain spillover.
levels.High: Direct effect on sea lanes, energy or shipping, a Singapore-flagged vessel affected, or relevance to deployments.

attentionScore.desc: Deterministic, explainable rank. state (Priority 40 / Active 25 / Watch 10 / Archive 0) + escalation risk (Severe 20 / High 15 / Moderate 8 / Low 2) + 5 per dimension that changed over the last 7 days (compareDays) + 10 if the state moved up over the same window + Singapore exposure (High 8 / Moderate 4 / Low 0) + tier (T1 6 / T2 3 / T3 0) + 8 if the live open-source feed shows a coverage surge (see definitions.feed.surgeRule). Items flagged ignore-for-now are shown but ranked last.

feed.source: GDELT DOC 2.0 API (open, no key). Per item: 30-day daily article counts (TimelineVolRaw) and the most relevant English-language articles of the last 7 days (ArtList, HybridRel). Synced by .github/workflows/sync-watchlist-feed.yml into watchlist-live.json.
feed.surgeRule: A coverage surge is flagged when the last 7 days carry at least twice the article volume of the 7 days before and at least 20 articles; a surge adds 8 points to the attention score.
feed.titleFilter: Articles are kept only when the title contains one of the item's terms, to cut GDELT's full-text noise.
feed.terms: Title filter: at least one of these substrings must appear in an article title for it to count as reporting on the item.
feed.require: Optional groups of substrings; a title must contain at least one term from every group (two-party theatres: one term per side).
feed.exclude: Optional substrings that drop a title (sport, entertainment and other noise), in addition to the sync's global list.
feed.spamDomainsNote: Article sources dropped outright (livestream/score spam). The daily review adds domains seen producing noise.

columns.tier: Standing relevance to the Army: T1 Priority Conflicts, T2 Active Regional & Escalation Watches, T3 Baseline Regional Research Reserve. Tiers do not change week to week.
columns.state: Today's monitoring state: Priority (direct strategic relevance or high Army learning value), Active (material trend, escalation or regional relevance), Watch (baseline monitoring), Archive (reserve; revisit on a named trigger). ▲▼ marks a move over the last 7 days.
columns.status: Current status: the newest title-matched headline from the live open-source feed (synced hourly) on top, then a plain-language summary of what is happening now whose first sentence states the newest development, with links to the newest reporting it rests on. The phase label sits beneath; a struck-through label is the phase 7 days ago.
columns.coverage: Open-source coverage from the live feed (GDELT with Google News fallback): the sparkline is the last 30 days (or four weekly counts), the number is articles in the last 7 days with the change against the 7 before. 'Surge' = at least twice the prior week and at least 20 articles. Refreshes hourly.
columns.nextIndicator: The soonest dated indicator to watch, tagged with the numbered topic and watch area it informs (or 'cross-cutting' when it bears on the theatre as a whole). Expand the row for the full list.
columns.confidence: How well-sourced the assessment is: High (multiple independent, dated sources), Medium (some single-source or snippet-only items), Low (thin or contested reporting).
columns.attention: Attention score, the register's sort order. Hover a score for its breakdown.
columns.topic: Topics of interest: the three capability contests the Army follows this theatre for, set by the team (from the watchlist workbook). Numbered so they line up with the 'Why it matters' and 'Watch areas' columns; the chip is the topic's adaptability rating.
columns.whyMatters: Why it matters here: for each numbered topic, what the theatre tests (the capability, behaviour or mechanism under study).
columns.watchAreas: Watch areas: for each numbered topic, its watch status and what to monitor. Status tags: Rising (activity increasing), Established (steady pattern), Contested (the outcome is still open), Watch for trigger (review only on a named event), Background monitor, Declining.
columns.adaptability: Adaptability: how transferable the topic's lessons are to the Army — High, Medium or Low, set by the team.

items.whyNow: With Lavrov (23 Sep) and Peskov (24 Sep) ruling out any pause or 'temporary settlement', the energy-strike truce Zelensky offered at the UN is dead for now and both deep-strike campaigns run into winter unchecked: Russia's 23–24 Sep raid killed 16 across Ukraine and Ukrainian drones reportedly reached Perm and Ulyanovsk on 25 Sep, while Vivaldi's robot-borne logistics sustain a local counteroffensive north of Lyman and Russian drones keep spilling into NATO and Moldovan airspace.
changes: 25 Sep: Ukrainian drones reportedly set the Perm refinery (~1,500 km from the border) ablaze and hit the Iskra electronics plant in Ulyanovsk, with explosions also reported in Voronezh; reported by the Exilenova Plus channel, with no comment yet from Ukraine's General Staff or Russian authorities (Kyiv Independent, single source). Overnight on 24 Sep drones hit oil depots in Rostov Oblast and Krasnodar Krai, the Rostov governor confirming debris damage while Moscow claimed 40 drones downed (Kyiv Independent).

24 Sep: Russia's night attack with 282 drones, four Zircons and three ballistic missiles in three waves killed 16 and injured 59 across Ukraine (two dead in Kyiv, eight in Donetsk Oblast, six in Kharkiv Oblast) and damaged a maternity hospital, energy and logistics sites; 227 targets were downed; Zelensky announced a 'very important' but undisclosed deal on a new batch of Patriot interceptors and warned that Ukraine will make winter 'painful for Russia as well' if energy strikes continue (Kyiv Independent, Ukrinform, Kyiv Post).

24 Sep: Kremlin spokesman Peskov said Moscow seeks 'peace, not a temporary ceasefire'; a day earlier Lavrov, after meeting Rubio in New York, said Russia 'will not pause the special military operation during negotiations in any format', while Rubio invited Putin to the G20 in Miami; ISW assessed the statements as an effective rejection of the US–Ukrainian limited energy ceasefire (New Voice of Ukraine, Meduza, ISW via Kyiv Post).

24 Sep: Suspected Russian drones crashed in Romania (Solca, after four minutes in its airspace) and Moldova (a Gerbera in Floresti), a day after a Russian Mi-8 spent 42 seconds in Polish airspace near Braniewo; ISW's 24 Sep special report counts at least 23 Romanian airspace violations in Jan–Aug 2026 against 18 in 2022–25, and Denmark's DDIS warned of a 'low but growing' risk of limited Russian strikes on NATO border states (Kyiv Independent, Euronews, ISW).

21 Sep: The CEC said United Russia took a record 355 of 450 Duma seats on 57.8% of the party-list vote at the 18–20 Sep elections; final results are due by 5 Oct, and ISW on 24 Sep described the vote in occupied Ukraine as a staged referendum on occupation (Moscow Times, Meduza, ISW).

20 Sep: Operation Vivaldi phase two retook Shandryholove, Derylove and Drobysheve; the 3rd Army Corps says 125 km² is under its control, 50 km² recaptured, robots ran 15,700 missions and 90% of frontline evacuations, and Russia's Rubicon drone formation was withdrawn after heavy losses (Kyiv Independent, Defence Matters, single source for the robot figures).

timeline.text: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held three-hour talks with Vladimir Putin in Moscow, then travelled to Kyiv under a three-day pause on strikes against both capitals.
Russia hit Kyiv with 32 cruise missiles and 166 Shahed-type drones, over half jet-powered, killing five and ending the pause declared during the US envoys' visit.
Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps revealed Operation Vivaldi, a counteroffensive near Lyman it said cleared 75 square kilometres of Russian infiltrators and liberated Serednie and nearby villages.
A Ukrainian drone strike set both crude distillation units ablaze at Gazprom Neft's Moscow refinery, halting processing for several weeks, Reuters reported citing industry sources.
Ukraine struck the Bashneft-UNPZ refinery in Ufa and the Kuibyshev refinery in Samara overnight, both more than 900 kilometres from the Ukrainian border, causing fires.
Zelensky met Trump at the UN General Assembly, said Ukraine is ready for a reciprocal energy ceasefire, and urged trilateral talks with Putin at the G20 in Miami.

After meeting Rubio in New York, Lavrov said Russia would not pause its military operation during negotiations in any format, while Peskov said the next day that Moscow seeks peace rather than a temporary ceasefire.
Russia launched 282 drones and three waves of ballistic and Zircon missiles, killing 16 people across Ukraine including two in Kyiv, while suspected Russian drones crashed in Romania and Moldova.

text: On persistent ISR versus signature management and deception, the Established and Contested status is borne out locally and contested in the information space. The 3rd Army Corps’ 20 Sep account of Vivaldi’s second phase credits ravine approaches and search-and-strike drone teams for surprise at Shandryholove, while on 23 Sep ISW read Russian encirclement claims as cognitive warfare. Deception works for one corps; whether it scales is open. On EW versus alternative UAS control and layered counter-UAS, the Rising rating holds and the pressure point has moved to ballistic missiles: the 23–24 Sep raid mixed 282 drones and decoys with Zircon and Iskander waves, 227 targets were downed yet 16 people died, and on 24 Sep Zelensky announced an undisclosed Patriot deal while Finland asked Musk for Starlink over Russia to reach launchers. Layered defence is now sought at the launcher too.

On contested sustainment versus dispersed support and repair, the Established and Contested status is borne out on both sides. Ukrainian drones reached Rostov and Krasnodar depots on 24 Sep and reportedly Perm and Ulyanovsk on 25 Sep (single source); Russia hit Kyiv energy and logistics on 24 Sep and Lavrov on 23 Sep ruled out any pause for talks. Endurance rests on repair speed and dispersal; the corps’ claim that robots ran 90% of evacuations (24 Sep, single source) shows where dispersed support preserves tempo.

items.name: Israel–Palestine (Gaza)

phase.now: Ceasefire without implementation; Yellow Line creep and targeted strikes

snapshots.phase: Phase 1 ceasefire, unresolved disarmament
Ceasefire without implementation; Yellow Line creep and targeted raids
Ceasefire without implementation; Yellow Line creep and targeted strikes

items.whyNow: UNGA week produced words, not implementation: Netanyahu on 24 Sep defended the war and set out no ceasefire steps, Hamas on 24–25 Sep demanded entry of the technocratic committee and the international force and called his speech 'lies and slogans', and Board of Peace envoy Mladenov told donors the $2.4bn plan is 'not working according to a timetable' while the health ministry's count since the truce reached 1,408 with five more killed in 24 hours.
changes: 25 Sep: Hamas dismissed Netanyahu's UN speech as 'lies and slogans', said the walkouts showed Israel's isolation and that his place is in prison, without announcing new steps on the roadmap (Palestinian Information Center, single source); EU foreign policy chief Kallas told the two-state alliance meeting that Gaza progress is 'far too limited' (Anadolu).

24 Sep: An Israeli strike on a vehicle at al-Baidar south-west of Gaza City killed one man and a second strike hit the vehicle carrying his body near Sheikh Ajleen, wounding relatives; two more were killed at al-Zahra and al-Zawaida in central Gaza (WAFA, Arab News). Gaza's health ministry put the toll at 73,928 since October 2023 and 1,408 killed and 4,916 wounded since the 10 Oct 2025 ceasefire, with five killed and 35 injured in 24 hours (TRT World).

24 Sep: Netanyahu told the UN General Assembly that genocide allegations are 'the biggest lie of the century' and that Israel 'prevented genocide', without setting out ceasefire implementation steps; Hamas spokesman Hazem Qassem said the movement is 'fully ready' to implement the Board of Peace roadmap, demanded entry of the technocratic committee and deployment of international forces, and accused Israel of 'complete obstruction' of the agreement (CBS, Jerusalem Post, TRT World).

24 Sep: At a UNGA side event Mladenov said the Board is 'not working according to a timetable', Maj-Gen Jasper Jeffers outlined area-by-area demilitarisation with IDF withdrawal only after verified demilitarisation of each zone, and the plan includes a permanent Rafah ISF site for 5,000 personnel (Jerusalem Post, single source for the force figures); UNCTAD put Gaza's recovery needs at $71.5bn with unemployment above 90% (Al Jazeera); Saudi envoy Manal Radwan told Egypt's 'Sharm El-Sheikh to Phase II' roundtable that aid must enter 'without obstacles or preconditions' before winter (Arab News).

23 Sep: The Board of Peace unveiled a $2.4bn, 66-project six-month reconstruction plan conditioned on Hamas disarmament, the same day an Israeli strike on a vehicle in western Khan Younis killed Hamas finance official Mohammad Abu Elwan and Osama Abu Khater, among seven killed that day (Al Jazeera, Reuters via US News).

22 Sep: Defence Minister Katz said the IDF will make no partial withdrawals from the 63% of Gaza it controls until Hamas is fully disarmed and threatened to destroy what remains of Gaza City and evacuate a million people if a single Israeli is kidnapped; on 21 Sep eight Arab and Islamic foreign ministers called on Israel to fulfil its Phase One commitments (Jerusalem Post, Turkish MFA via GlobalSecurity).

timeline.text: The UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2803, endorsing the US Gaza plan, welcoming the Board of Peace and authorising an International Stabilization Force for Gaza.
Israel's security cabinet approved entry of an initial International Stabilization Force of about 200 personnel from countries such as Uganda and Morocco, operating in coordination with the IDF.
Hamas approved the Board of Peace's plan pairing gradual disarmament with phased Israeli withdrawal, a plan Netanyahu rejected pending genuine disarmament.
An Israeli-backed raid in Gaza City detained the head of Hamas's internal security service; airstrikes covering the withdrawal killed at least five Palestinians, including two children.
Kosovo signed a Participating Country Agreement for the International Stabilization Force in Pristina, while Board of Peace envoy Mladenov admitted implementation was 'not there yet'.
UN humanitarian officials said Israel had pushed the yellow line inward, leaving Palestinians under 40 percent of Gaza, with 1,334 killed since the ceasefire.

The Board of Peace unveiled a $2.4bn, 66-project reconstruction plan conditioned on Hamas disarmament, while an Israeli strike in western Khan Younis killed senior Hamas finance official Mohammad Abu Elwan among seven dead that day.

Netanyahu told the UN General Assembly that genocide allegations are the biggest lie of the century, while Hamas said it was fully ready to implement the roadmap and demanded entry of the technocratic committee and deployment of the international force.

text: On dense urban operations versus dispersed and concealed networks, the Established and Contested status is borne out by method rather than scale. On 23 Sep a vehicle strike in Khan Younis killed finance official Mohammad Abu Elwan, on 24 Sep a vehicle at al-Baidar was struck twice, the second time while carrying the first victim’s body (WAFA, single source), and a 600-metre tunnel found on 23 Sep shows the network still moves beneath the Yellow Line; Jeffers’ 24 Sep area-by-area demilitarisation model leaves verification untested. On persistent ISR and precision strike versus civilian protection and legitimacy, the Contested status is confirmed at the strategic-information level: Netanyahu on 24 Sep rebutted the genocide charge rather than describe implementation, Hamas on 25 Sep answered with ‘lies and slogans’, and Kallas on 25 Sep called progress ‘far too limited’. With 1,408 killed since the truce by 24 Sep, targeting freedom buys local effects at a rising legitimacy cost.

On humanitarian access versus operational control, the Established status holds and access is a bargaining chip: Katz on 22 Sep ruled out withdrawal from the 63% the IDF holds until full disarmament, Mladenov on 24 Sep said the $2.4bn plan runs to no timetable, Hamas demanded the technocratic committee and ISF be let in, and UNCTAD put recovery needs at $71.5bn. Entry control, not capacity, governs endurance into winter.

items.whyNow: Iran tabled a written road map on 23 Sep (60-day regionwide ceasefire, phased Hormuz reopening, end of the blockade) and on 25 Sep its security chief Mohsen Rezaei gave Washington four to five days to accept it 'completely and all at once', while Reuters reported a phased Hormuz-for-blockade deal under discussion and the Senate failed 49–50 to curb the war. The Strait stays effectively closed (ten commodity vessels on 24 Sep against a ten-day average of 17), the Cape Dao was hit on 23 Sep with one seafarer killed, Brent settled at $106.60, and Singapore's crude route runs through the contested waters.
changes: 25 Sep: SNSC secretary Mohsen Rezaei said 'Talk is enough… Now we must act', giving Washington four to five days to meet Iran's conditions (declared commitment to diplomacy, negotiation timetable, sanctions relief, end of operations on all fronts) before Hormuz reopens or talks proceed; Rubio said it would be wrong to call the UNGA contacts a breakthrough; Bloomberg counted ten commodity vessels through the strait on 24 Sep against a ten-day average of 17; no US answer to the road map had been reported by 25 Sep (Gulf News, straits.live).

24 Sep: Reuters sources said US and Iranian negotiators in New York were exploring a staged deal in which Iran reopens Hormuz and Washington lifts the economic blockade, with neither side willing to give up leverage first; an 80-country group led by Bahrain demanded full restoration of navigation; Pezeshkian told Fox News 'America must choose' and that 'the Houthis are responsible for their own actions' (Reuters via Yahoo, Iran International, Arab News).

24 Sep: The Senate failed 49–50 to advance the Iran war-powers resolution (Collins, Murkowski, Paul, Tillis for; Fetterman against); Brent settled up 3.4% at $106.60 after a $108.23 session high on the Houthi barrage at Saudi Arabia, easing on the phased-deal report; WTI $94.61 (CNBC, NPR).

Salam told the UN on 24 Sep that Lebanon wants no vacuum after UNIFIL and a Council-mandated monitoring presence, Macron backed a replacement on 23 Sep, and a six-month extension is reported stalled (single source). With about 30 Israeli positions counted on 22 Sep and Hezbollah re-entering pockets of the line, verification contracts as reconstitution is claimed; adaptability stays Medium.

On distributed maritime posture versus force protection, the Rising · Contested rating stands: an eleven-ship multinational formation operated for six days under observation without interference, but the civilian-flagged fisheries fleet remains the exposed element, as the 18 Sep collision showed, and Taiwan's 100-tonne cutter at Pratas adds another lightly protected outpost. timeline.text: A Hague Court of Arbitration unanimously rules the Indus Waters Treaty remains fully in force and bars India from raising the Ratle dam; India rejects the award within hours as 'illegally constituted'.
Pakistani troops fire small arms and mortars across the Line of Control in Poonch's Mankote sector, a day after firing in Krishna Ghati; the Indian Army retaliates.
Indian destroyer INS Kolkata and Pakistani patrol vessel PNS Hunain collide in the North Arabian Sea during Pakistan's SEASPARK-26 exercise, the first physical military incident since May 2025.

India and Pakistan each summon the other's charge d'affaires over the collision; Pakistan calls it 'belligerent Indian action', India calls the Pakistani ship's conduct 'unacceptable and unprofessional'.
Two Pakistani Jaish-e-Mohammad militants are killed overnight in 'Operation Sohan' in the Majalta forests of Udhampur, Jammu, and a suspected over-ground worker is detained.
India rejects Pakistan's version of the warship collision as 'the usual prevarication', insisting INS Kolkata was on routine surveillance in international waters.

Dar tells the OIC Contact Group in New York that the Indus treaty is binding and cites the August award, India rejects the group's Kashmir communiqué, and New Delhi signs a contract for 160 satellite-guided anti-airfield weapons.

India's envoy at the UN Human Rights Council tells Pakistan that 'neither terror nor theatrics' will repay its loans and demands it vacate the parts of Jammu and Kashmir it holds, as New Delhi restates that the Indus arbitration court is illegally constituted.

text: On cross-border strike and counterstrike versus escalation management, the Established · Contested status held without a kinetic test: after the 15 Sep Arabian Sea collision both navies settled into competing narratives, the last move being India’s 18 Sep rebuttal, and the only Line of Control reporting between 18 and 25 Sep was three mines defused in Poonch on 23 Sep. Signalling has moved to hardware and exercises: the 23 Sep contract for 160 satellite-guided anti-airfield glide bombs and Tarang Shakti at Jodhpur from 26 Sep with US F-35s keep India’s stand-off airfield-strike option visible, while Trump’s 22 Sep claim to have ended the May 2025 war shows the escalation-management story itself is contested. On counterterrorism versus interstate deterrence, the Established rating rests on words, not casualties: India’s 24 Sep UNHRC reply tied Pakistan to ‘exporting terror’, Sharif declined questions on Hafiz Saeed at UN headquarters on 24 Sep, and no attack followed the 17 Sep Udhampur encounter.

On air, missile and information operations versus nuclear-threshold ambiguity, the Contested edge is argued rather than tested: Dar’s 23 Sep OIC statement, India’s 24 Sep restatement that the arbitration court is illegal, Rubio’s 23 Sep remark and a 25 Sep Strategic Plans Division workshop (single source) all treat a repeat crisis as plausible. Adaptability stays High but unexercised; the window’s only adaptation is India’s turn to lawfare and stand-off munitions.

timeline.text: Min Aung Hlaing is inaugurated as president of Myanmar's quasi-civilian military government at the parliament complex in Naypyitaw.
Min Aung Hlaing offers peace talks to armed groups with a 100-day deadline ending 31 July; the Karen National Union, Chin National Front and National Unity Government reject it.
The military launches 'Operation 4926', a combined land, naval and air offensive against the Arakan Army across Sittwe, Ponnagyun, Kyaukphyu and Gwa townships in Rakhine State.
Six fibre-optic FPV drones strike Tada-U airbase near Mandalay; resistance says Yak-130 jets were hit, the junta says all were intercepted, and international flights are cancelled.
The Arakan Army's counter-offensive seizes four junta outposts on the Sittwe-Ponnagyun border, including positions near Minchaung Bridge and the Shwe Min Gan naval station.

A junta column of over 180 vehicles and about 1,000 troops with MLRS, drones and signal jammers reaches the DDI 25 weapons plant in Saw Township to renew the offensive on Mindat and Kanpetlet in southern Chin State.
An Air Force strike on a truck rest stop at Sattawkone village on the Mandalay-Myitkyina highway in Indaw Township kills two civilians and destroys two trucks.

The Arakan Army repels a two-week junta attempt to breach the Maei mountain pass at Mindon into Rakhine, Malaysia sets a 29 Sep date to begin deporting Myanmar migrants after Anwar invites Min Aung Hlaing for an official visit, and Myanmar recalls its ambassador to Thailand for questioning.

text: On distributed resistance versus state airpower, the Established · Contested status holds and airpower keeps substituting for ground movement that fails: the battalion-scale push through the Maei pass at Mindon, begun 10 Sep under daily air and paramotor strikes, was repelled by 24 Sep (single source), while the 1,000-troop column with MLRS and jammers staged at DDI 25 on 20 Sep has not yet moved on Mindat or Kanpetlet. Strikes on quiet areas at Myit Chay (13–18 Sep, 4,000 displaced), Indaw on 23 Sep and four Rakhine townships on 21–23 Sep, alongside the NUG’s 23 Sep count of 20,383 regime dead since mid-2024 (single source), show no force-generation advantage accruing to the regime. On commercial UAS and improvised systems versus conventional advantage, the Rising status is borne out but cuts both ways: regime kamikaze drones killed 20-plus Karenni civilians in September (single source), columns carry jammers and the 18 Sep bail of an American charged with teaching Kuki-Chin fighters drone assembly and jamming shows a transnational training pipeline.

On fragmented governance versus logistics and civilian resilience, the Established status is confirmed: Bangladesh’s 25 Sep UNGA plan, Malaysia’s 29 Sep deportation start and Anwar’s invitation to Min Aung Hlaing, the 24 Sep ambassador recall from Bangkok (single source) and Mizoram’s lifted embargo on 24 Sep show corridors and refugee flows becoming bargaining objects that neighbours, not the regime, shape.

items.whyNow: On 24 Sep the Houthis fired a mixed missile and drone barrage at Jazan, Yanbu, Taif and Riyadh, Saudi Arabia intercepted six ballistic missiles with alerts issued for Mecca and Jeddah, France announced soldiers, radars and air-defence systems for the Yanbu terminal, and the Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish foreign ministers met in New York under the Makkah defence pact and agreed to convene their chiefs of staff. Fighting for the heights above Bab al-Mandab continues, Iraq's coalition presence is down to Erbil airport ahead of the 30 Sep exit, and Brent settled at $106.60.
changes: 25 Sep: Reports confirmed that the Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish foreign ministers (Faisal bin Farhan, Ishaq Dar, Hakan Fidan) met in New York on 24 Sep under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, condemned the attacks on Mecca and agreed to hold an urgent meeting of the three chiefs of staff on support for Saudi Arabia; Iran's President Pezeshkian told Fox News 'the Houthis are responsible for their own actions' (Arab News, Reuters via WHBL).

24 Sep: The Houthis claimed 'dozens of ballistic missiles and drones' at Saudi military sites in Jazan (Al-Tuwal, Al-Daghareer camp) plus ballistic and cruise missiles and drones at a 'sensitive target' in Riyadh and Aramco facilities in Yanbu, asserting hundreds of Saudi casualties (unverified claim); the coalition said six ballistic missiles aimed at Taif and Yanbu were intercepted and civil-defence alerts covered Mecca, Jeddah, Yanbu, Taif and Tabuk (Anadolu, France 24).

24 Sep: President Macron said France will 'send military assets, meaning soldiers, radars and defence systems' to protect the Yanbu oil terminal, with no timeline given; Brent settled up 3.4% at $106.60 after a $108.23 session high on the barrage (Arab News, France 24, CNBC).

24 Sep: Yemeni government forces repelled overnight Houthi infiltration attempts on the Taiz–Aden supply route (al-Ashbout, Heijah al-Abd, Al Ahkum); WHO counts 674 killed and almost 3,000 injured since 6 Aug with 164 deaths in 13–18 Sep alone and 158,000 displaced; at least 150 fighters were killed in 24 hours on the heights overlooking Bab al-Mandab, where the Giants Brigades had retaken positions around Kahboub on 21–22 Sep (Al Jazeera, France 24, Asharq Al-Awsat).

24 Sep: Coalition forces in Iraq are now present only at Erbil airport ahead of the 30 Sep exit, with 1 Oct declared 'Sovereignty Day'; Baghdad's plan announced 22 Sep moves militia disarmament to June 2027 behind a 90-day halt in attacks, which Kataib Hezbollah and Nujaba reject until foreign troops leave; Israeli forces assaulted a shepherd during an incursion between Al-Asha and Al-Rafid in Quneitra (SANA, single source) after Sharaa said on 22 Sep that security talks had reached about 90% before Israel pulled back (Arab News, The National, Kurdistan24, MEMO, Anews).

18 Sep: Lloyd's List Intelligence counted 1,165 Bab el Mandeb transits in August, down 49% month on month, with only one Saudi-linked tanker through since the 20 Jul embargo, and judged the Houthis' new coastal holdings improve their ability to observe and strike shipping (Lloyd's List Intelligence).

timeline.text: The Houthis declare a naval and air blockade of Saudi Arabia in response to a strike on Sanaa airport, ending four years of relative calm under the 2022 truce.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi says 30 September is the 'fixed and final' date for ending the US-led coalition mission and completing the withdrawal of its forces.
Israel strikes Syria's Abu al-Duhur airbase in Idlib, saying it aims to prevent a Turkish military deployment; Damascus and Ankara deny the claim.
Drones launched from Iraq's Maysan province hit Saudi Arabia's East-West crude pipeline in Riyadh and Medina provinces; Riyadh shuts the line the next day and Brent tops $100.
Houthi forces seize Perim Island and the last stretch of Yemen's Red Sea coast a day after taking Mocha, gaining control of Bab al-Mandab and reiterating a ban on Saudi ships.
The Houthis fire a ballistic missile and drones at Riyadh for the first time in this escalation; Saudi Arabia says it was intercepted as smoke rises near King Khalid airport.

Iraq's prime minister moves militia disarmament to a phased plan ending in June 2027 behind a 90-day halt in attacks, as Syrian President Sharaa says security talks with Israel reached about 90 percent before Israel pulled back.

text: On long-range attack versus layered protection, the Rising · Contested status is borne out. On 24 Sep the Houthis fired ballistic and cruise missiles and drones at Jazan, Yanbu, Taif and Riyadh, Saudi forces reported six ballistic interceptions; France answered the same evening with soldiers, radars and defence systems for Yanbu, while the Makkah pact partners agreed only to convene chiefs of staff. Point defence holds over cities, but a European detachment at the terminal shows Saudi layered coverage is stretched; the Houthi claim of hundreds of Saudi casualties is unverified. On maritime disruption versus route resilience, the Established · Contested status is confirmed on land: fighting for the Kahboub heights and the Taiz–Aden pass on 22–24 Sep killed about 150 fighters in a day, Lloyd's List on 18 Sep counted August Bab el Mandeb transits down 49 percent month on month, and Brent's $106.60 settle on 24 Sep priced Yanbu rather than the strait.

On regional basing versus militia targeting, the Established · Contested status is shifting toward host-nation management: coalition forces are down to Erbil airport before the 30 Sep exit, Baghdad has moved militia disarmament to June 2027 behind a 90-day ceasefire that Kataib Hezbollah and Nujaba reject, and Israeli incursions into Quneitra continued on 24 Sep (single source) while Sharaa says talks reached 90 percent. Posture is renegotiated politically; the kinetic pattern holds.
